title: FPGA Digital Alarm Clock
summary: An FSM-driven digital alarm clock built on an FPGA, with mode control, a live clock, and time and alarm setting.
specs: CORE: Cyclone V FPGA · LANG: VHDL · TEAM: 2
content:
ENSC 252 course project · Simon Fraser University · Team of 2 (with Sumair Amrala)

View more details on GitHub →

Role

Co-designer and developer (design, VHDL implementation and testing, split equally)

My Tasks

  • Co-built a full FSM-driven 24-hour alarm clock on an FPGA with three modes: running, set time and alarm set.

  • Implemented debounced, edge-detected button logic using a two-stage shift register, so each key press registers as exactly one clean pulse.

  • Built reusable BCD counter modules (0–59 and 0–23) from custom D flip-flops with independent hold, increment, synchronous and asynchronous reset.

  • Integrated modular VHDL sub-systems through a shared control interface between the counter, editing and display logic.

  • Verified every module with ModelSim testbenches and on-board testing on the DE10-Standard.

How It Works

Key Specs

  • Hardware: Cyclone V FPGA (DE10-Standard), written in VHDL with Intel Quartus Prime and ModelSim

  • Timing: 50 MHz board clock prescaled by a 25-bit counter (÷ 2²⁵) to a ≈1 Hz tick

  • Modes: Running, Set Time and Alarm Set, chosen with SW1/SW0 and shown on LEDs 0–2

  • Controls: KEY1 increments, KEY2 moves between hours/minutes/seconds, KEY0 confirms or stops the alarm, KEY3 hard resets

  • Display: 24-hour time on six 7-segment displays (HH:MM:SS)

  • Alarm: triggers only when armed and the current time matches; LED3 shows armed, five LEDs light when it goes off

In Action

Left: running mode on the DE10-Standard, with 24-hour time on the six 7-segment displays. Right: the alarm going off at 00:01:00, with the LEDs lit once the armed alarm matches the current time.

title: AI Posture Detection System
summary: A live webcam app that detects poor posture and alerts the user. It advanced to the Greater Vancouver Regional Science Fair.
specs: CV: OpenCV + MediaPipe · LANG: Python · RESULT: Science fair finalist
content:
Independent project · Greater Vancouver Regional Science Fair finalist

Role

  • Built a live webcam app in Python that detects slouching and alerts the user in real time.

  • Gathered and labelled roughly 1,500 good- and poor-posture images using Google’s Teachable Machine.

  • Used MediaPipe to extract body and face landmarks, exporting each frame’s coordinates to a CSV dataset with Pandas.

  • Trained and compared four scikit-learn classifiers (Logistic Regression, Ridge, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting) across two trials in Jupyter.

  • Presented the project as a finalist at the Greater Vancouver Regional Science Fair.

How It Works

MediaPipe Pose’s 33 body landmarks. Each frame’s x, y and z coordinates became one row of training data. (Diagram: Google MediaPipe)

Results

Across two trials, the four models scored between 64% and 88.5% on test data, and their rankings swung noticeably from one trial to the next:

In live use, the detector was right about 60–70% of the time. The large swings between trials, such as Gradient Boosting dropping from 88.5% to 74.3% while Ridge jumped from 64.2% to 81.6%, showed the dataset was too small and too uniform for the models to learn posture reliably. The biggest lesson was that a model is only as good as how varied its data is. Next time I’d collect samples from more people, camera angles and lighting conditions.

In Action

The detector tested on sample posture photos: good posture (left) and poor posture (right), each with the predicted class and the model’s confidence.

Key Specs

  • Language: Python in Jupyter Notebook

  • Computer vision: OpenCV for the webcam feed, MediaPipe for pose and face landmarks

  • Data: images labelled in Google’s Teachable Machine; landmark coordinates stored as CSV and handled with Pandas

  • Models: Logistic Regression, Ridge Classifier, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting (scikit-learn)

  • Output: real-time Good / Poor posture label with the model’s probability

Built on Nicholas Renotte’s Body Language Decoder tutorial.

title: Automatic Blueberry Sorter
summary: A motor-driven sorter that classifies blueberries by size and filters out non-conforming objects in real time.
category: TCS3200 COLOR SENSOR · SG90 SERVO · ELECTRIC MOTORS
specs: SENSOR: TCS3200 · DRIVE: 12V DC + SG90 servo · ROLE: Project manager (team of 8)
content:
ENSC 100W design lab project · Simon Fraser University · Team of 8

Role

Project Manager

My Tasks

  • Designed a motor-driven centrifugal sorting mechanism to automate the physical separation of blueberries.

  • Led the integration of a TCS3200 color recognition sensor with a MiuZei SG90 servo motor, building the color detection and rejection system:

    • Sensing: the TCS3200 reads the RGB values of each berry from within 10 mm.

    • Classification: readings are compared against a calibrated blueberry range of RGB(25, 35, 105) to RGB(100, 160, 235).

    • Actuation: anything outside the range triggers the SG90 servo to sweep a 30° flap, diverting it into the reject hole.

How It Works

Key Specs

  • Feed motor: 12V DC motor (200 RPM, 0.44 N·m) with an L298 driver to tune the speed

  • Color detection: TCS3200 sensor, accurate within 10 mm

  • Rejection: MiuZei SG90 servo at 6.0 V driving a 4 cm flap over a 4 cm reject hole

  • Size sorting: small (8 × 10 mm) and large (18 × 20 mm) slots along a quarter-circle branch

  • Output: 3 cm tunnels for accepted berries and a pull-out rejection tray; the system disassembles for washing

Presenting the Blueberry Sorter 9000 with my team of 8 at the ENSC 100W design showcase, Simon Fraser University.

title: Split
summary: A phone app for eating out with friends: AI finds restaurants that fit the whole group, plans the order within budget, and splits the bill by what each person actually ate.
specs: STACK: HTML, CSS, JavaScript · AI: Gemini + Cloudflare Worker · EVENT: ProtoHacks
content:
ProtoHacks hackathon · Team of 4

Try the app → View the code on GitHub → Devpost →

Every time we eat out with friends, the same three problems come up: nobody can agree on where to go, somebody goes over budget, and the bill gets split evenly even though one person had a salad and another had a steak and two drinks. Split handles the whole night, from picking the place to paying each other back.

What It Does

  • Group: everyone enters their budget, cuisine, distance and diet. Split uses AI to search for real restaurants, ranks them by how many people they work for, then the group votes.

  • Planner: snap a photo of the menu, enter the headcount and budget, and get an order that fits after tax and tip.

  • Fair Split: snap the receipt, everyone taps what they ate, and tax, tip and discounts are split by what each person ordered. Payment requests go out by e-Transfer, PayPal or Venmo.

  • Ledger: past meals, who owes who, and how much you've spent.

It's a web app you add to your home screen, so it works on iPhone and Android with no app store.

How We Built It

  • Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework or build step, so the whole team could edit right away.

  • Google Gemini reads menus and receipts from photos and searches the web for restaurants.

  • A Cloudflare Worker holds the Gemini API key, so it never ends up in the public repo or in users' browsers.

  • Firebase Realtime Database syncs the group live between phones, and GitHub Pages hosts the app.

The Math Behind the Fair Split

Each person pays for their own food plus a share of the extras (tax + tip − discounts) proportional to what they ordered, so the salad person pays less tax and tip than the steak person. Money is handled in whole cents, with leftover pennies going to the biggest remainders, so the shares always add up to the bill exactly. For the planner, the food can cost at most budget ÷ (1 + tax rate + tip rate).

Challenges

  • Keeping the API key secret: GitHub Pages can only serve files, so the live site was stuck in demo mode until we moved the key to a Cloudflare Worker.

  • Four people pushing to one repo meant merge conflicts and overwritten work, so we got a lot better at stashing, pulling and resolving conflicts.

  • Gemini sometimes returned "high demand" errors, so we kept a demo mode with sample data as a backup for the presentation.

title: Animu
summary: A web app that turns your Spotify music into an aesthetic backdrop: when an anime song plays, it finds the matching opening and loops it full-screen behind your music.
category: JAVASCRIPT · NODE.JS · SPOTIFY API · ANIMETHEMES API
specs: RUNTIME: Node.js · APIs: Spotify + AnimeThemes · TYPE: Personal
content:
Personal project · Built for fun

View the code on GitHub →

I wanted my music to feel like the anime it came from. Animu watches what you’re playing on Spotify, and when an anime song comes on it finds that show’s opening and loops it full-screen behind the music, so your screen becomes a living backdrop. I use it regularly while I study.

Role

  • Designed the whole system myself: planned the pipeline, worked out how each part should behave and chose the tools and APIs, then built it with the help of AI-assisted coding.

  • Designed the Spotify connection with PKCE sign-in (no client secret), following the current track and device and sending playback controls back to Spotify.

  • Planned the matching logic that searches the AnimeThemes catalog by song title and artist credits, with title normalization and fallbacks when there’s no direct match.

  • Designed a local video cache that downloads each opening once, streams it while it loads and keeps the cache under 3 GB by removing the least recently watched videos.

How It Works

If a song doesn’t match an opening directly, Animu uses the track and album info to work out which anime it’s from and shows its first opening instead. If that also fails, the song’s cover art becomes the background. A dim slider darkens the video without blurring it, so it stays easy on the eyes.

In Action

Two songs, two openings: the dim slider on the right darkens the video (left) or lets it shine through (right), with now-playing info and playback controls along the bottom.

Setup and Controls

The one-time Spotify setup using secure PKCE sign-in (left; my client ID is blurred out), and the built-in guide to the controls (right).

Key Specs

  • Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, installable as an app

  • Server: Node.js, serving the app locally and caching videos

  • APIs: Spotify Web API (PKCE sign-in), AnimeThemes API

  • Matching: title normalization and artist-credit matching, with album and cover-art fallbacks

  • Cache: videos downloaded once and streamed, capped at 3 GB with least-recently-watched removal

Disclaimer: Animu is a personal, non-commercial project. Anime openings are streamed from AnimeThemes and belong to their respective copyright holders.

title: Sakura Assistant
summary: An anime desktop companion that makes focusing fun. Focus sessions and finished tasks earn points that unlock new characters, outfits and backgrounds.
specs: BACKEND: Python (FastAPI) · AI: Gemini + ElevenLabs · EVENT: StormHacks 2026
content:
StormHacks 2026 hackathon · Team of 4

View the code on GitHub → Devpost →

Productivity tools often feel cold. Sakura Assistant makes focusing fun: a 3D anime companion talks with you, keeps you on task and rewards real work. Focus sessions and finished tasks earn Sakura Petals, which you spend to unlock new characters and to customize their outfits and backgrounds.

Role

  • Designed and built the 3D character models from scratch in VRoid Studio, including their outfits and accessories.

  • Built the Python (FastAPI) backend with AI-assisted coding: the game rules, petal rewards and save file, the quest and schedule system, and the focus watcher.

  • Connected the backend to Google’s Gemini LLM for in-character conversation, and to ElevenLabs for each character’s English and Japanese voice.

How It Works

Each character has its own Gemini system prompt, so it stays in persona while still taking real actions such as adding a quest or scheduling a session. To keep replies feeling instant, the backend splits Gemini’s reply into sentences, sends each one to ElevenLabs as soon as it’s ready and saves every generated line for reuse.

Focus Mode

Start a focus session and the timer runs. Open a blocked app or website and your companion scolds you, takes away petals and closes the distraction.

Rewards and Summons

Petals earned from focus and quests are spent on summons, which can unlock new characters. Real work unlocks rewards, not real money.

Characters and Customization

The collection of nine characters (left), and the dressing room where outfits, headwear, eyewear and backgrounds are swapped (right).

Companion and Quests

The home screen (left), and a conversation where the character reacts to your pending tasks and deadlines (right).

Key Specs

  • Backend: Python with FastAPI

  • AI: Google Gemini for chat, planning and character personas

  • Voice: ElevenLabs text-to-speech, speech-to-text and sound effects, in English and Japanese

  • Characters: 3D models made in VRoid Studio, rendered with three.js and three-vrm

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript desktop app for Windows

Disclaimer: Sakura Assistant was built only for the hackathon and is not released for public use. Several characters are fan-made recreations of characters from existing anime, and those characters belong to their respective copyright holders.
